extracted.intended_audience: Department of Defense managers, policy makers, medical facility commanders, and efficiency review/performance analysts involved in evaluating or improving military medical care productivity
extracted.subtask_short: efficiency review for military medical care
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for measuring productivity and conducting Efficiency Reviews (ER) and Performance Work Statements (PWS) within Department of Defense medical care functions, including limits of existing indices and procedural requirements for A-76/ER processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: CWU/FTE index limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The CWU/FTE index is a single factor productivity measure that cannot fully reflect changes in output caused by inputs other than labor, and because changes in output cannot be wholly explained by changes in labor input, the CWU/FTE index is not useful for management to separate differences in operational efficiency from differences in patient characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary conclusion: the CWU fails to provide valid, useful information to management and does not meaningfully aid in the identification of areas for potential productivity improvement. The index's reliance on labor as the sole input makes it invalid for many managerial purposes without extensive qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCU (Health Care Unit) inadequacy / case-mix adjustment failure
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCU is ineffective in assigning proper weights to illnesses according to severity and the requirement for medical resources; because of differences in case mix among military facilities and services, the HCU (as currently developed) and the CWU are inadequate to properly adjust for case mix differences and therefore inappropriate for intra- and inter-Service productivity comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Navy nonconcurrence: improvement is negligible; use of indices that fail to weight severity will 'signal inefficiency' incorrectly across the Military Health Services System. Case-mix differences must be addressed or indices will misrepresent productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of productivity trend statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity trends reported (e.g., BLS and DOD figures) are frequently questionable due to flawed underlying data and measures; quality of productivity measurement is affected by the suitability of output measures, comprehensiveness of output measurement, and accuracy/usefulness of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports frequently offer lengthy qualifications explaining trend values (e.g., too few variables in CWU, inability to reflect change). Users should treat aggregated trend statistics cautiously and examine underlying measures, variable selection, and data accuracy before drawing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Input measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Inputs for the health care facility are usually measured as manpower (dollars per hour), beds (dollars per bed), or in terms of total resource cost (labor, supplies, facilities, utilities, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which input(s) are used and the monetary basis; recognize that many functions use outputs that are actually intermediate or input-like, which can distort resource allocation if tied to funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Output has commonly been measured in terms of dollars per patient day or output per unit of input. An alternative approach treats the patient as the input (admissions or outpatient visits) and output as patient days; then productivity can be represented by average length of stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All such measures have been criticized for failing to represent facility and functional output adequately. Choose output measures carefully and be aware of their implicit assumptions (e.g., patient homogeneity) and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of single-factor measures; need for total/partial factor approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on partial or single-factor productivity measures (such as labor productivity ratios) is problematic; total resource allocation decisions are being influenced by measures at hand for lack of better information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A holistic approach to productivity measurement (total or partial factor productivity) is recommended because many output measures used are actually inputs or intermediate outputs subject to manipulation when tied to resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics required of a 'better' productivity measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A better measure must consider or adjust for: 1) patient arrivals (admissions/outpatient visits) generate workload; 2) patient characteristics (demographics, disease, etc.) affect resource use; 3) available resources described in dollar terms (facilities, labor, supplies, utilities); 4) organizational characteristics (structure, policies, style of practice, size, capacity) directly affect patient care processes; 5) output quantity must be relatable to quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a measure should obtain the quantity and type of patients by disease distribution and the respective total cost in resources to produce appropriate goods/services for defined outputs at an acceptable level of quality after adjustment for organizational characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) requirements (OMB A-76 / DOD guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB Circular A-76 required each Federal activity to develop performance requirement standards and performance indicators suitable for use equally by contracting organizations and in-house providers. PWS 'describes what work is to be done without stating how to do it' and identifies standards of performance to be met in measurable terms and defines allowable variance from those standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS should set predefined standards for quantity, quality and timeliness; be used as the basis for organizational review and cost-comparison studies; and include a performance requirements summary outlining all performance indicators, standards and accepted quality levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS must include quality assurance plan and performance requirement summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph A.2.c of Enclosure 3, DODI 5010.XX requires PWSs be developed in accordance with OFPP Pamphlet No. 4 and must include a quality assurance plan and a performance requirement summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those functions without standard measurable output would have difficulty implementing such requirements; quality assurance plans should demonstrate how effective and efficient an activity is in meeting performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: PWS pricing and staffing-mix requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph A.2.e of DODI 5010.XX requires the 'pricing of those tasks (those identified in the PWS) in terms of manhours, material, and equipment and formulating an effective mix of staffing patterns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taken literally, this implies procedures similar to cost-comparison efforts of the CA program; this effort can be time consuming, expensive, and stressful to the local workforce and may resemble full cost-comparison studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up audit requirement for ER/PWS actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclosure 3 requires follow-up audits be conducted (Paragraphs A.g gq and h.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive follow-up audits similar to CA cost-comparison studies can be costly and may overshadow expected savings; plan audits considering cost vs. benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: ER program periodicity and labor standard updates (DODI 5010.XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft DODI 5010.XX stated that 'all activities (of DOD) are to be reviewed by the end of FY 87 and at least once every five years thereafter...labor standards will be updated every three years.' Components shall allocate resources based on the most recent staffing or labor standards and summarize to justify PPBS requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ER implementation requires substantial manyear resources; compliance timeframes imply heavy workload to implement reviews across all functional areas on the mandated schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: ER suitability criterion: definability and measurability of tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency Review is most successful in activity areas that are essentially well-defined and where tasks are easy to observe and measure. ER processes are especially suitable for tasks that are easily defined, whose inputs and products are identifiable and quantitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military medical treatment facilities often have poorly defined products that are hard to quantify; such areas pose formidable barriers to successful ER application.

rubrics_metrics.name: General limitations and contextual factors affecting ER in military medical settings
rubrics_metrics.description: ER faces problems such as differences from profit-motivated private industry; need to consider wartime standby requirements and career/retention patterns; need for higher-level approvals for many changes; political and managerial resistance to personnel reductions; lack of incentives for employee involvement in productivity improvement; and risk of overlapping/conflicting manpower figures if not integrated with other programs (CA, manpower requirements determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for long lead times, political/union resistance, and integration across programs. ER success hinges on top-down support and careful long-term planning with relocation/incentive strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: ER team composition and process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When Medical Care is selected for ER, assemble a team of about 6-8 persons: two trained analysts, at least one representative of the major claimant, and the rest functional expert workers who have relevant training. General approach: draft Preliminary ER Plan; prepare ER Performance Work Statement; conduct ER Functional Analysis; develop and submit ER Study Report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During preliminary planning, use all available information (regulations, org manuals, civilian literature), conduct site visits as necessary, and undertake economic analysis to identify areas with best cost-containment potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic analysis focus in ER (selection of target areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: An economic analysis is usually conducted by the ER team to identify specific activities or areas within the functional area offering the best chances for cost-containment savings. Congressional interest may influence choice (e.g., outpatient utilization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams should investigate utilization causation (why patients seek care) to determine legitimate care and potential opportunities for savings; be cautious about assumptions (e.g., over-utilization assertions) and require evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data requirement: population/demographic information (DEERS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful demographic data (beneficiary status, age, sex) are essential to evaluate utilization causation and for resource planning, management, and allocation. DEERS was developed to provide such catchment-area beneficiary estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DEERS or equivalent reliable demographic sources when analyzing utilization and planning resource allocation; recognize that facilities differ substantially in beneficiary mixes which affects productivity and service needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donabedian indicators for identifying service-requiring potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Donabedian listed several phenomena that indicate and can represent service-requiring potential: 1) people, 2) mortality or survival, 3) morbidity, 4) situations that require care but cannot be classified as morbidity or mortality, and 5) health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a multi-faceted set of indicators (not single counts) when determining legitimate service needs and utilization drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems with organizational and technological change for ER
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected changes in weapons or other technologies often markedly impact organizational and functional structure; ER would require a new base review for such changes. Similarly, rapid tech changes can negate labor standards overnight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ER programs must plan for technological change and allow for frequent updates to standards; static base reviews may become obsolete quickly in dynamic environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/complexity trade-offs of OFPP Pamphlet No.4 methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: OFPP Pamphlet No.4 sets forth a formalized, highly structured methodology that is time- and labor-intensive. Service-related and mission/geographical differences make the ER process expensive for many CA activities, with potential short-term losses from these efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for high implementation costs and possible short-term negative impacts; weigh expected savings against resource requirements before initiating full-scale application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns/criteria to address when contracting-out (CA program issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies showed CA successes but identified issues to be addressed when contracting out: 1) job security for Federal workers; 2) quality of services rendered; 3) validity of standard cost-comparison values; 4) who decides which CA functions are exempt; 5) short-term vs. long-term budget impacts; 6) political, legislative, and regulatory restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering contracting out, explicitly evaluate these social, quality, and governance concerns alongside cost comparisons and efficiency metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming homogeneity of patients and services
rubrics_metrics.description: CWU, HCU and comparable civilian equivalents assume that patients and the goods/services rendered are homogeneous, yet cannot adequately account for organizational structural, process, technological differences or change, nor relate well to measures of output quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on measures that assume patient/service homogeneity. Adjust measures for case mix, organizational context, and quality dimensions before using them for management or resource-allocation decisions.
